newsitem.title: USA: US/foreign yield spreads seen little fazed by Fed.
newsitem.headline: US/foreign yield spreads seen little fazed by Fed.

text.p: Interest rate differentials between U.S. and overseas bond markets are expected to remain relatively steady in the wake of the Federal Reserve's credit tightening on Tuesday, international market analysts said.
"I think ... it is all built in," said Chris Widness, international economist at Chase Manhattan Bank.

"There are big enough events occurring overseas, especially with regard to fiscal policy, that it is hard to see markets expecting overseas interest rates to be rising in the wake of the Fed hike," he added.
Government bond markets in Japan, Great Britain, Germany and much of Europe had effectively discounted the Fed's 25-basis-point snugging of the federal funds rate on Tuesday, experts said.

Major bond markets, including the U.S., were steady but firmer, in the run up to the U.S. central bank's Federal Open Market Committee meeting. U.S. Treasury bonds wavered after after the Fed announced the new fed funds target of 5.50 percent. Within minutes of the news, the benchmark 30-year bond dipped then rose, then slipped again, but its yield never strayed far from 6.90 percent.

UK gilts and other "English speaking" markets are most highly correlated with the U.S. bond market and should track Treasuries more closely than German bunds or Japanese JGBs, at least in the near term, said Richard Koss, international strategist at MFR Inc, an investment advisory firm.
"The problem is if Treasuries don't change, then the gilts won't be any more unchanged than the bunds," Koss quipped.

Moreover, the dollar's exchange rate has not yet reached a lofty enough level to prompt foreign central banks, especially the Bundesbank and Bank of Japan, to preempt more favorable dollar spreads by following the Fed's lead, strategists said.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke sowed a bit of confusion in the market on Monday, telling German radio he hoped U.S. rates would remain steady, adding that an increase in U.S. rates could push German rates higher.
But most analysts said they thought he was referring to German market interest rates, not making an overt hint about Bundesbank policy.

"The market is not going to get too buzzed up on the idea there is going to be any interest rate response from central banks outside of the U.S. Therefore, the impact on respective bond markets is relatively limited," said Alan Ruskin, research director at market consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
Japanese JGBs are essentially on their own tangent, decoupled from other markets mainly because of yearend flows ahead of Japan's March 31 financial year end, Ruskin said.
Spread-wise, the core European markets were more tightly linked to German bunds than to U.S. Treasuries, he added.
MFR's Koss said the yield advantage that 10-year U.S. Treasury notes hold over the same duration bund could narrow a few basis points from its current premium of around 93.

He said Japanese and European investors reportedly had an appetite for U.S. two-year notes at Tuesday's Treasury auction, indicating that foreign demand should limit any Treasury market weakness in the near term.
"The overall sense is the Fed is ahead of this game," Koss said. "The dollar markets continue to look attractive."
But analysts said the U.S. bond market is still jittery about the timing of the next U.S. credit tightening.
"Until you get the all-clear signal, it's not going to rally too much, it's just that foreign flows should limit any losses," Koss said.
